title: Redis in Production
subtitle: Monitoring, security, and operational best practices
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Redis is deceptively simple to run in development but has critical production pitfalls: open by default with no authentication, dangerous commands like FLUSHALL available to anyone, and performance issues that only manifest under load.
whyItExists.solution: A production Redis checklist: enable authentication, bind to a private network, disable dangerous commands, set memory limits with eviction, enable persistence, monitor memory and latency, and use slow log for diagnostics.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Before launching any Redis instance accessible from the internet or shared infrastructure. These practices prevent security breaches, data loss, and production incidents.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Local development Redis (localhost only) doesn't need all of this — but build good habits early.

explainModes.beginner: Running Redis in production is like running a restaurant. You need locks on the doors (authentication), smoke alarms (monitoring), rules about how much food to keep (memory limits), and a backup generator (persistence). Without these, things go wrong in expensive ways.
explainModes.simple: Production checklist: set a strong password (requirepass), bind to private IP, rename or disable dangerous commands (FLUSHALL, DEBUG), set maxmemory with an eviction policy, enable persistence, monitor INFO memory and slow log.
explainModes.standard: Security: requirepass, bind to private IP, TLS, rename/disable dangerous commands with rename-command. Performance: maxmemory + eviction, slow log, latency monitoring. Ops: INFO ALL metrics, MONITOR for debugging (not in production), keyspace notifications for event-driven patterns. Sizing: set maxmemory to 70% of RAM to leave headroom for fork() and OS buffers.
explainModes.technical: Redis AUTH (password) and ACLs (Access Control Lists, Redis 6+) control access. ACLs let you grant per-command and per-keyspace permissions per user. TLS is natively supported since Redis 6.0. Rename-command in redis.conf aliases or disables commands at the protocol level. Latency monitoring (LATENCY HISTORY, LATENCY LATEST) tracks event latency. MEMORY USAGE key returns bytes for a specific key.
explainModes.deepDive: Redis 6+ ACL system supports fine-grained rules: ACLS with ~keypattern and &channelpattern and +command -command. Redis 7.0 added ACL LOG for audit trails. For high-performance production, disable Transparent Huge Pages (THP) on Linux — Redis's memory allocation pattern causes THP to fragment and slow down fork(). Set vm.overcommit_memory=1 to allow Redis to safely fork even when not all pages are physical. Use numactl to pin Redis to a single NUMA node.

content.text: Redis has no authentication by default. An internet-exposed Redis is a critical vulnerability — attackers can read all data, overwrite keys, or achieve remote code execution via config manipulation. Always secure before deploying.

content.code:
# redis.conf — Security settings

# 1. Bind to private/localhost only (NOT 0.0.0.0)
bind 127.0.0.1
# Or bind to private IP only: bind 10.0.1.5

# 2. Require password
requirepass "use-a-long-random-password-here"

# 3. Enable TLS (Redis 6+)
tls-port 6380
tls-cert-file /etc/redis/redis.crt
tls-key-file /etc/redis/redis.key
tls-ca-cert-file /etc/redis/ca.crt

# 4. Disable dangerous commands
rename-command FLUSHALL ""
rename-command FLUSHDB  ""
rename-command DEBUG    ""
rename-command CONFIG   "CONFIG-ADMIN-ONLY-SECRET"

# 5. Disable protected-mode if binding explicitly
protected-mode yes  # keep enabled if bind not set

content.text: Redis 6+ supports ACLs — per-user permissions on commands and key patterns. This lets you give the app only what it needs, not full admin access.

content.code:
# Create a restricted app user
redis-cli ACL SETUSER appuser on >app-password ~* +GET +SET +DEL +EXPIRE +TTL
# on = enabled
# > = password
# ~* = access all keys
# + = allow these commands only

# Create a read-only user
redis-cli ACL SETUSER readonly on >readonly-password ~* +@read

# List ACL users
redis-cli ACL LIST

# Check current user
redis-cli ACL WHOAMI

# ACLs in redis.conf
# user appuser on >password ~cache:* +GET +SET +EXPIRE

# redis.conf — Memory settings

# Set to 70-80% of available RAM
maxmemory 3gb

# Eviction policy for cache workloads
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

# LRU sample accuracy (higher = more accurate, more CPU)
maxmemory-samples 10

# Check memory usage
redis-cli INFO memory
# used_memory_human: 1.50G
# mem_fragmentation_ratio: 1.08  (ideal: 1.0-1.5)

# Check memory for a specific key
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE mykey SAMPLES 5

# Find big keys
redis-cli --bigkeys

# Key metrics via INFO
redis-cli INFO memory     # memory usage
redis-cli INFO stats      # commands/sec, hits/misses
redis-cli INFO keyspace   # key count per database
redis-cli INFO replication # replication status
redis-cli INFO clients    # connected clients, blocked

# Cache hit rate (from INFO stats)
# keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses)

# Slow log — commands taking > 10ms
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10
redis-cli CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 10000  # microseconds

# Latency monitoring
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST
redis-cli LATENCY HISTORY event

# Real-time command stream (dev/debug only!)
# redis-cli MONITOR   # DO NOT run in production — huge performance impact

# 1. Disable Transparent Huge Pages (causes latency spikes)
echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

# 2. Allow overcommit memory (required for fork/RDB)
sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1
echo 'vm.overcommit_memory = 1' >> /etc/sysctl.conf

# 3. Increase max connections
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65535

# 4. Add to /etc/rc.local for persistence
echo 'echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled' >> /etc/rc.local

# Redis will warn about these in startup log if not set

items: Set requirepass with a strong password (or use ACLs)
Bind to private IP only — never 0.0.0.0 in production
Set maxmemory to 70% of RAM and choose an eviction policy
Set up Sentinel or Cluster for HA
Monitor hit rate, memory, and slow log continuously
Disable Transparent Huge Pages and set vm.overcommit_memory=1 on Linux

content.text: Never run MONITOR in production — it logs every command and significantly degrades performance. Use SLOWLOG GET for identifying slow commands instead.

questions.question: What command shows the slowest recent Redis commands?
questions.explanation: SLOWLOG GET returns recent commands that exceeded the slowlog-log-slower-than threshold (default 10ms). Use it to identify performance bottlenecks.

questions.question: Why should you disable Transparent Huge Pages on Linux for Redis?
options: Redis doesn't support large memory pages
THP causes memory fragmentation and latency spikes during Redis fork() for RDB saves
THP conflicts with Redis's password authentication
THP is only for database workloads, not caches
questions.explanation: Redis's fork-based RDB save uses copy-on-write memory. THP (Transparent Huge Pages) causes the OS to split huge pages on copy, adding significant latency and memory fragmentation. Disabling THP is a standard Redis production recommendation.

questions.question: What is the recommended maxmemory setting relative to available RAM?
questions.explanation: Set maxmemory to 70-80% of available RAM. Leave headroom for the fork() child process during RDB saves (copy-on-write can temporarily double memory), OS page cache, and other system processes.

faq.q: What is a good maxmemory setting?
faq.a: Set maxmemory to 70-80% of available RAM to leave headroom for fork() during RDB saves, OS page cache, and OS buffers. With 8GB RAM, set maxmemory to 5-6GB.

faq.q: How do I find which keys are using the most memory?
faq.a: Run redis-cli --bigkeys (scans keyspace, reports largest per type). For a specific key: MEMORY USAGE key SAMPLES 5. For the whole instance: INFO memory shows used_memory and fragmentation.

faq.q: Should I use Redis AUTH or ACLs?
faq.a: Redis 6+ ACLs are more powerful: they allow per-user command and key-pattern restrictions. For new deployments, prefer ACLs over the single global requirepass password. Use requirepass for compatibility with older Redis versions.

examples: Locking down Redis at a startup: requirepass + bind to VPC subnet + rename FLUSHALL to '' prevented a data wipe during a misconfiguration incident
Using ACLs to give the app only +GET +SET +EXPIRE and a read-only user for analytics
